formulas.name: Price Elasticity of Demand
formulas.formula: PED = (% Change Qty Demanded) / (% Change Price)
formulas.analyst_note: Rarely calculate with formula. Observe pricing events and track volume response in next 1-2 quarters. Consistent price hikes without volume loss = demonstrated inelastic demand = strongest buy signal.
formulas.worked_example: Airtel raises recharge Rs 199 to Rs 219 (+10.1%). Subscribers drop 35.5cr to 34.8cr (-2.0%). PED = -2.0%/10.1% = -0.20. Highly inelastic -- strong pricing power.

formulas.name: Price Elasticity of Demand
formulas.formula: PED = (% Change Qty Demanded) / (% Change Price)

variables.meaning: Price Elasticity of Demand; measures responsiveness of quantity demanded to price changes
Percentage change in quantity demanded = ((New Qty − Old Qty) / Old Qty) × 100
Percentage change in price = ((New Price − Old Price) / Old Price) × 100

formulas.plain_english: PED tells you how much customers' buying behaviour changes when you raise or lower price. A PED of −0.5 means a 10% price increase cuts sales by only 5%, revealing inelastic demand—the holy grail for margins. PED < −1 signals elastic demand, where price hikes backfire. For equity research, observing PED through pricing actions is more revealing than any survey.
formulas.analyst_note: Rarely calculate with formula. Observe pricing events and track volume response in next 1-2 quarters. Consistent price hikes without volume loss = demonstrated inelastic demand = strongest buy signal.

worked_example.problem: Airtel raises recharge Rs 199 to Rs 219. Subscribers drop 35.5 cr to 34.8 cr next quarter. Calculate PED and interpret.
worked_example.insight: A 10% price increase causes only 2% volume loss. This demonstrates strong pricing power—Airtel can raise prices without proportional customer loss. For equity research: inelastic demand (|PED| < 1) signals durable competitive advantage and margin expansion potential. This is a strong buy signal.

formulas.name: Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI)

variables.meaning: Herfindahl-Hirschman Index; measure of market concentration ranging from near-0 (highly fragmented) to 10,000 (monopoly)
Each firm's percentage share of total market revenue or volume

formulas.plain_english: HHI quantifies whether an industry is fragmented (many equal competitors) or concentrated (few dominant players). Higher HHI = fewer firms control more sales = less price competition = pricing power. In India, telecom HHI shifted from ~1,500 (2014, 9 players) to ~3,100 (2023, 3 players), enabling tariff hikes. HHI > 2,500 signals oligopoly—watch for tacit collusion on pricing.
computation: Obtain each competitor's market share (as percentage of total market)
Sum all squared values to get HHI
Note: HHI is unitless; use benchmarks below to interpret

worked_example.problem: Indian Telecom market (2023): Jio 40%, Airtel 33%, Vi 20%, Others 7%. Calculate HHI and assess competitive intensity.
worked_example.insight: At 3,138, Indian telecom is a tight 3-player oligopoly well above the 2,500 threshold. This extreme concentration explains the 2021–2023 tariff increases (+25–40%) with minimal subscriber loss. For equity analysts: consolidation → HHI rise → pricing power → margin expansion. Jio and Airtel are in a durable duopoly; Vi's lower share and legacy cost structure make it vulnerable.

formulas.name: Lerner Index

variables.meaning: Average selling price per unit of product or service
Incremental cost to produce one additional unit; approximated as COGS/volume for steady-state operations

formulas.plain_english: The Lerner Index measures the percentage markup on marginal cost relative to price. A Lerner of 0.6 means 60% of the price is pure markup—pricing power in action. Perfect competition yields Lerner ≈ 0 (price = marginal cost); monopolies often exceed 0.7. For equity research, rising Lerner signals durable competitive advantage (brand, patent, network effects). Watch for compression if competition intensifies.
formulas.interpretation: 0.6 = 60% of price is markup. Luxury brands and patent-protected pharma often above 0.7.

worked_example.problem: Asian Paints sells 1-litre Premium Emulsion at ₹500. Annual cost of goods sold is ₹120 crores on 3 crore litres sold. Estimate Lerner Index and interpret.
steps: Marginal Cost per unit = ₹120 crores / 3 crore litres = ₹40 per litre
worked_example.insight: A Lerner of 0.92 reveals exceptional pricing power: 92% of the price is markup over marginal cost. This near-monopoly level reflects Asian Paints' brand strength, distribution network, and customer switching costs in India's organised paint market. Such high Lerner is sustainable only with continued brand investment and innovation. Compare: if a generic paint maker has Lerner = 0.3, Asian Paints' 0.92 justifies a premium valuation multiple.
